rationale: The replication failure is already on the page, but not where the experiment is described, and the maintenance tag pointing to it is attached to a sentence the replication did not test. Correcting the small setting error and adding one attributed sentence right after the walking-speed description resolves the tag and stops the Wikipedia article from saying two different things about the same experiment.

The sentence says people judged an interviewer after holding a drink before an interview, but the cited paper had no interview: participants rated a fictional person described on paper. The sentence should be corrected to what the study did, and a later attempt to repeat that experiment, which found no effect, can be reported in one attributed sentence.

The paper is cited in the lead for the claim that the speed of priming is contested, but it is about unconsciously activated goals and says nothing about such a dispute. Removing this reference from that sentence is the smallest accurate change; the sentence keeps its other reference.

Two sentences describe the experiment as comparing two groups of people, but the paper states that the same people judged both outcomes. Rewording them to match the paper is a small, uncontroversial correction; the finding itself stands and has been replicated.

The quotation and its attribution are correct, and a later replication with more data and more leagues found the same thing. One attributed sentence could report that, but the Wikipedia article is not wrong without it.

The paragraph presents the 2006 result as promising evidence, but later attempts to repeat the exercise in other schools, one of them a direct replication of this study, found no effect on grades. Readers are missing that, so a short attributed addition after the two sentences on the study is recommended.

The sentence is broadly right but leaves out a condition the paper stresses: the diversity statement mattered only when the company's brochure showed few minority staff. The replication on file tested a different experiment from the same paper, so it gives no reason to change what the Wikipedia article says.

The Wikipedia article cites this paper only for background statements, which the paper supports. The later check simply re-ran the paper's own calculations successfully, which is not something a reader of this Wikipedia article needs to be told.

The Wikipedia article is right as it stands: the 1997 survey results held up when repeated in 2021 with a larger sample. Adding one sentence about that replication is optional and would simply show readers that the key evidence has been independently confirmed.

The Wikipedia article says the study showed gamers have better hand–eye coordination and resist distraction, but the study measured visual attention and found gamers were more affected by distractors, not less. Rewording the sentence to what the study found, and attaching the same reference to the next sentence, makes both sentences accurate and removes a 'citation needed' tag.

The Wikipedia article reports Plott and Zeiler's claim that the buying-selling price gap comes from flawed experimental procedures, but not that a later direct replication of their experiment still found the gap. One attributed sentence after the Plott and Zeiler sentence would tell readers this.

The Wikipedia article states that the original study has never been replicated, but a 2014 replication with 396 participants exists and did not find the effect. The sentence should be corrected and the replication's result reported with attribution.

The sentence that cites this paper is correct. The later reanalysis questions a different part of the paper, its finding that weak institutions fully explain the paradox, so adding that finding together with the reanalysis is optional enrichment of the Wikipedia article's paragraph on institutions.

The Wikipedia article only says that the game has been studied, which is true, so nothing needs correcting. Because the page is about the game, a reader would benefit from two attributed sentences saying what the 2020 experiment reported and what the 2023 replication of it found, including that players also became less willing to believe true tweets.

The sentence is accurate and the confirming replication is already cited beside it. A contributor who wants the section to say what the research found could add one attributed sentence on the 2019 evaluation, including that it had no control group.

The 2018 paper tested an earlier card-based classroom game, not the Bad News browser game, so it does not support a sentence about research on Bad News. Taking this one reference off the sentence fixes the mismatch, and the sentence remains supported by the other studies cited there.

Two sentences attribute to the cited paper things it does not say (that waiting to see the kick is better, and that goalkeepers dive to please teammates and win recognition), so the paragraph should be brought back to what the paper reported. A 2026 replication that directly tested the finding and did not find an advantage to staying in the centre is missing and can be added in one attributed sentence.

The replication is already covered. A few details of the original experiment are misreported: the length of the zoo trip, what group 3 was asked, and which statistical comparisons the authors made. Correcting them brings the paragraph in line with the paper.

The Wikipedia article's use of the study is accurate, and a large later replication of the study's experiment found the same pattern with a smaller effect. Mentioning the experiment and its replication would enrich the example but is not needed for accuracy.

The Wikipedia article presents this study as an example of defaults shaping consent, but a large direct replication did not find the default effect and found that the wording of the question mattered instead. One attributed sentence after the list would tell readers that this example did not hold up when repeated.

The Wikipedia article says the lips position made participants frown, but the cited study says it only prevented smiling, which is the point of the design (smiling inhibited versus smiling facilitated). The replication findings are already covered, so the only change needed is to correct that description.

The replication mostly confirms what the Wikipedia article says about Sachs and Warner's finding, so nothing in the Wikipedia article is wrong or missing contrary evidence. One attributed sentence on the replication, backed by a survey that also describes it, would be an optional enrichment.

The replication evidence is already well covered, so nothing needs adding there. The one problem is a sentence that attributes to the original authors a conclusion (lasting hormonal changes, wage negotiations) that their paper does not state; it should be narrowed to what the paper says.

page_title: Big Five personality traits and culture
rationale: The Wikipedia article says the study compared cultures in Europe, but the paper's countries span several continents. The fix is to drop 'in Europe' and describe the comparison as the paper does; the rest of the passage matches the source.

The cited study found that absences fell by a quarter in one Kenyan programme, which is not the same as attendance rising by 25 percent, and it does not support a general statement about deworming programs. The sentence should be reworded to match the study, and a re-analysis of the same data that weakened part of the result can be mentioned alongside it.

The sentence only says that national accounts data are used to study economic growth, and the cited paper does exactly that. The later re-estimation of the paper's results has no bearing on this sentence.

The sentence claims more than its sources say: they report evidence of p-hacking and publication bias that differs by research method, not that the reliability of economics as a whole was being undermined. Restating the sentence as what the studies found keeps the point and removes the overstatement.

The Wikipedia article mentions the ESP paper only as an example of a controversy, and what it says about the paper is correct. Adding that a large replication did not find the effect would help readers see why the paper became a cautionary case, but the Wikipedia article is not wrong without it.

The sentence only says that security researchers have applied the theory to workplace behaviour, and the cited paper is a clear example of that. The replication's mixed results concern details of the paper's model that the Wikipedia article does not mention.

The two examples in the list match what the cited paper reported, and a large 2021 replication found the same results. Adding the replication is optional: it would show readers that these examples have held up, but nothing in the Wikipedia article is wrong without it.

The Wikipedia article reports the paper's finding correctly, and re-running the authors' analysis gave the same result, so the content stays as it is. The one error is the second author's name, which is misspelt in the sentence and should read 'Urbatsch'.

The figures the Wikipedia article gives for Asch's 1956 study match the paper. Recent replications found nearly the same rate of conforming answers, so a one-sentence mention would show readers that the result still holds; it is optional because nothing in the Wikipedia article is wrong.

The section's main evidence that daydreaming boosts creativity is one 2012 experiment, and a larger later attempt to repeat that experiment did not find the effect. Readers should be told this in one attributed sentence.

No change is needed on account of the replication, which succeeded and concerns a finding the Wikipedia article does not mention. The explanation of 'moral patient' attributed to this paper is not in it and mixes up the two concepts the section is trying to distinguish, so it should be replaced with the paper's actual definition.

The Wikipedia article is accurate. The same paper also ran an experiment showing the default itself changes what people choose, and a larger 2023 replication found the same, so one optional sentence could strengthen the claim that the default causes the gap.

The sentence says anger signals limits in a negotiation, which the cited paper reports. The replications tested a separate finding about when anger backfires, which this Wikipedia article never states, so there is nothing to correct or add.

A recent, larger repeat of this study mostly confirmed the finding but with weaker effects, and it did not appear in the questions about stock prices. One attributed sentence would let readers know the bias is real but less uniform than the Wikipedia article's flat statement suggests.

The Wikipedia article quotes the original experiment's striking result (twice as many agreeing to donate under opt-out). A much larger repeat of that experiment confirmed that defaults matter but found a clearly smaller difference, and a one-sentence, attributed addition would tell readers so.

The Wikipedia article only says she published work on this topic, which is true. A later study that did not reproduce one paper's result belongs in an article about the effect, not in the researcher's biography.

The sentence about the liquidity-risk paper is correct and needs no change. In the same paragraph, however, two references attached to the sentence about work with Pástor and Taylor point to unrelated papers by other authors and should be swapped for the two Pástor–Stambaugh–Taylor papers already listed in the Wikipedia article's bibliography.

The biography only says what the study was about, and that description matches the paper. The replication source is a pooled analysis that does not discuss this study individually, so there is nothing to add or correct.

The biography describes the 2004 paper's findings correctly. A later comment disputes how well the result holds for the very largest cities, but that debate belongs in the articles on Gibrat's law and Zipf's law rather than in a one-sentence summary of the author's work.

The Wikipedia article does not use this paper as evidence for any finding; it lists it as a retracted paper, which the retraction notice confirms. A failed replication of a paper the Wikipedia article already presents as retracted adds nothing the reader needs in this biography.
The Wikipedia article only names the model and cites the paper that introduced it, which is accurate. The replication is about the paper's experiment, not about anything this biography says.

The page is a biography that only says what the paper examined and found, and the paper supports that description. Replication results belong in articles about the finding, not in an author's biography, and here the replication found the same gender gap anyway.

The sentence only says who traced the diabetes signal to this gene, and the cited paper supports that. The later Iranian study found the same association, which the Wikipedia article already treats as well established, so adding one more small confirming study would not improve the Wikipedia article.

The 2011 paper cited for this sentence is a laboratory and mouse study and says nothing about clinical trials, so half of the sentence has no source. A 2017 paper we found does say that several BET inhibitors were in clinical trials at that time, so the clause can be dated and given that source.

The Wikipedia article's statements match what the cited paper reports. The replication attempt partly reproduced the finding and was otherwise inconclusive for technical reasons, and it is only available as a preprint that was rejected by the journal, which is not a suitable source for a Wikipedia article about a cancer-drug mechanism.

The Wikipedia article says oxytocin given as a nasal spray increased empathy in healthy men, which is what the cited study reports, and a later study found the same. Adding one more single study to a medical-style claim would not improve the Wikipedia article, and no review covering it was found among the checked sources.

page_title: List of common misconceptions about arts and culture
rationale: The list entry describes the 1993 study accurately and already says that later studies gave mixed results. The linked replication is one small study that found the effect, which the entry's phrase "mixed results" already covers.
The definition agrees with the cited paper, and the replication found the same effect, so there is nothing to correct or add in a list entry.

The cited Milgram paper shows people following an authority's orders; it says nothing about people rating an authority's opinion as more accurate. Either the definition should be worded to match what the source shows, or the sentence is left resting on a source that only supports half of it.
The definition matches the cited paper in simplified form. The mixed replication is relevant to the Distinction bias article, not to a one-line list entry.
The definition matches the cited paper. A non-significant replication of one experiment matters for the Cheerleader effect article, but does not make a one-line list definition inaccurate.
The definition agrees with the cited paper and the replication found the same effect, so no edit is needed.
The definition agrees with the cited paper and the replication found the same effect, so no edit is needed.
The definition agrees with the cited paper and the replications found the effect, so no edit is needed.
The entry correctly records that Stroop introduced the colour-word task in 1935. The replication confirmed the effect, and a timeline line does not need replication details.

page_title: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
rationale: The row only records who won the 2007 Nutrition prize and for which paper, and the reference points to the right paper. The later replication largely confirmed the finding, and a list of prize winners is not the place to report it.

page_title: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
rationale: The row only records who won the 2026 Economics prize and for which paper, and the reference matches the paper. The failed replications concern the finding itself and belong in articles that use the study as evidence, not in a list of prize winners.

page_title: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
rationale: The row already tells readers that the original finding failed to replicate and cites sources for both the finding and the replication. There is nothing to correct.

page_title: List of Ig Nobel Prize winners
rationale: The row only records who won the 2016 Peace prize and for which paper, and it does so accurately. The later study is about the finding, which the list does not describe.
The study is only listed among her publications and no sentence depends on it. The later replication by the same authors broadly supported the finding, so there is nothing to correct.
The Wikipedia article's figures for the CASS4 variant match the cited paper. The linked replication studies are about three other genes, so they have no bearing on what this Wikipedia article says.

The claim is correct and a large, preregistered replication found the same result. One attributed sentence reporting that replication would strengthen the passage, but nothing in the Wikipedia article is wrong without it.
The paper is listed in the references but not used for any statement in the Wikipedia article, and its replication confirmed the original result. No edit is warranted.

The cited finding is correctly described and a large preregistered replication found it again. A single attributed sentence could be added to show the result has held up, but the Wikipedia article is not wrong without it.
The lead describes the 1997 study correctly, and the replication is already listed in the Wikipedia article on the side its own abstract supports. There is nothing to add or fix.

The cited study followed one group of seventh graders for two years and looked only at maths grades, but the Wikipedia article presents it as a lasting, general academic advantage 'after several years'. A later, larger near-replication in university students found no link between mindset and grades, which readers are not told.

The Wikipedia article is accurate and already mentions both a critique and the 2015 reanalysis, so nothing is wrong. The reanalysis sentence could simply say what the study did (it re-ran Putnam's own data) and what a later review made of it.

The Wikipedia article already tells readers that this experiment was replicated several times without finding the effect, and its description of both the original and the replications matches the papers. The one thing worth a moment of a contributor's time is a wrong journal name in the reference.

The Wikipedia article says the original authors lost confidence in their 2012 findings in general, but the letter it cites says this about one experiment only, the one both replications tested. The paragraph should name that experiment and limit the authors' statement to it; the second author's name also needs correcting to Norenzayan.

The Wikipedia article uses this paper correctly, as a failed replication of the 2012 experiment. The later study linked to it is about a different topic (scarcity), so it gives no reason to change this sentence.
